result: Catalytically inactive PLD2 (xPLD2) inhibits TREK-1 mechanically evoked currents in HEK293T cells. Overexpression of xPLD2 reduced mechanically evoked TREK-1 currents by over 80% (from 0.181 ± 0.04 to 0.035 ± 0.013 pA/µm²), and truncation of the TREK-1 C-terminus (which binds PLD2) similarly decreased pressure-induced current by more than 85%. The C-terminus is essential for TREK-1 mechanosensitivity in cellular membranes.
evaluation: All reviewers accepted this finding without challenge. Reviewer 1 states 'the authors convincingly show that the application of shear to a cell can lead to changes in the distribution of TREK-1 and the enzyme PhospholipaseD2' and notes 'The activation of TREK-1 by mechanical stimuli was shown to be sensitized by the presence of PLD2, but not a catalytically inactive xPLD2 mutant.' The editor notes 'The data provide solid evidence' for the mechanism. No concerns were raised about the electrophysiology data or the role of xPLD2.

result: Shear forces cause TREK-1 to redistribute from GM1 lipid domains to PIP2 clusters. Before shear, TREK-1 and GM1 displayed robust correlation, which significantly diminished after shear (p<0.01 at 50 nm). Conversely, TREK-1/PIP2 correlation was initially low but significantly increased after shear. With xPLD2, TREK-1 left GM1 domains after shear but showed weak association with PIP2 clusters.
evaluation: Reviewers 1 and 2 both explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 2 states 'The authors convincingly demonstrate that, post application of shear, an alteration in the distribution of TREK-1 and mPLD2 (in HEK293T cells) from being correlated with GM1 defined domains (no shear) to increased correlation with PIP2 defined membrane domains (post shear).' Reviewer 1 notes 'These movements are affected by TREK-1 C-terminal or PLD2 mutations suggesting that the interaction is important for channel re-location.' The super-resolution imaging data supporting these claims was praised.

result: PLD2 redistributes from GM1 to PIP2 clusters upon shear application. Prior to shear, PLD2 exhibited strong association with GM1 clusters, but after shear, PLD2/GM1 correlation decreased significantly while PLD2/PIP2 correlation robustly increased.
evaluation: This finding is explicitly supported by reviewers. The editor states 'the application of shear to cells causes a redistribution of both TREK-1 and an associated enzyme, PhospholipaseD2 in the membrane that increases the enzyme activity.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the activity of PLD2 is increased when the molecule is more associated with PIP2, rather than GM1 defined lipid domains.' No concerns were raised about the dSTORM imaging data showing PLD2 redistribution.

result: Shear forces reduce GM1 cluster size and free cholesterol levels. GM1 cluster size decreased from 167 ± 3 to 131 ± 3 nm (~20%) after shear in C2C12 cells. Free cholesterol levels in N2a cells decreased by 25% (p<0.001) after orbital shear, and this decrease was statistically significant (p<0.0001) and reversible within ~30 seconds.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly requests 'verification of the cholesterol assay, either by additional experiment or by citations of independent work,' indicating uncertainty about this measurement. While the GM1 cluster size data was not specifically challenged, the cholesterol measurement—which is mechanistically linked—requires additional validation according to the reviewer. The reversibility data was not questioned but depends on the validity of the cholesterol assay.

result: Cholesterol loading increases TREK-1 clustering with GM1 and inhibits TREK-1 currents. Lipidated apoE induced substantial clustering of TREK-1 with GM1 lipids in C2C12 cells, and fluid shear (3 dynes/cm²) completely reversed this effect. TREK-1 current density decreased nearly 2.5-fold in cholesterol-loaded cells (p<0.05).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'The authors additionally demonstrate that cellular uptake of cholesterol inhibits TREK-1 activation.' The dSTORM and electrophysiology data supporting this claim were not challenged. While Reviewer 3 requested verification of the cholesterol assay method, the functional consequence (reduced TREK-1 current) and imaging data showing increased GM1 clustering were accepted.

result: Depletion of cholesterol from astrocytes releases TREK-1 from GM1 lipids in mouse brain. In flox control mice (wild-type SREBP2), TREK-1 clustered near GM1, but in mice with astrocyte-specific SREBP2 deficiency, TREK-1 displayed reduced association with GM1 lipids (p<0.0001).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'in ex vivo studies, that depletion of cholesterol from astrocytes reduces correlation of TREK-1 and G1 lipids in mouse brain slices.' This finding was not challenged by any reviewer. The use of SREBP2 knockout mice to manipulate cholesterol levels was accepted as a valid approach, and the dSTORM data from brain slices was not questioned.

result: Osmotic stretch activates PLD2 and causes its redistribution from GM1 to PIP2 clusters. Membrane stretch by 70 mOsm swell led to ~50% increase in PLD2 activity in N2a cells, and dSTORM experiments demonstrated a shift in PLD2 spatial distribution from GM1 to PIP2 clusters after osmotic stretch.
evaluation: This finding extends the shear stress results to osmotic stretch and was not challenged by reviewers. The editor notes 'the application of shear to cells causes a redistribution of both TREK-1 and an associated enzyme, PhospholipaseD2 in the membrane that increases the enzyme activity,' which encompasses both mechanical modalities. The consistency across different mechanical stimuli was viewed positively.

result: PLD depletion in Drosophila increases mechanosensitivity and sensory responses. GM1 domains are present in fly brains, and dPLD responds to shear stress in fly cells (fourfold increase in activity). PLDnull flies exhibited lower arousal threshold to mechanical stimulation, and neuronal knockdown of PLD yielded similar mechanosensitivity increases. PLDnull flies also showed heightened sensitivity to electric shock.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'In vivo studies, using Drosophila melanogaster behavioural assays, were used to demonstrate that disrupting PLD2 altered behavioural responses to mechanical and electrical inputs.' However, the reviewer notes 'as the authors note, there is no TREK-1 homologue in this organism: thus the identity of the downstream effectors of PLD in D. melanogaster remain unknown.' Despite this limitation, the behavioral data demonstrating PLD's role in mechanosensitivity was accepted. The finding supports PLD's conserved role in mechanosensation even without identifying the downstream effector.

result: The mechanism involves van der Waals bonds between PLD2 palmitate moieties and GM1 lipids, and disruption of these bonds is necessary for PLD2 to dissociate from GM1 lipids, suggesting a 'shear thinning' mechanism within GM1 clusters.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'The claim on "shear thinning" is still very confusing. First, asymmetric insertion of molecules to one monolayer of the membrane is a main mechanism for membrane bending and curvature formation. Second, why is "shear thinning" equivalent to entropy/order?' This indicates the mechanistic interpretation remains unclear and potentially problematic. While the redistribution data is accepted, the specific molecular mechanism proposed is questioned.

result: The overall mechanistic model: PLD2 is a mechanosensitive enzyme regulated by GM1/cholesterol domains. Mechanical force deforms ordered lipids, disrupting PLD2-GM1 interaction, allowing TREK-1/PLD2 complex to associate with PIP2 clusters. This activates PLD2 to produce PA, which gates TREK-1.
evaluation: The editor states 'This important study poses a provocative mechanism of channel activation' and 'The data provide solid evidence' for the mechanism. Reviewer 1 concludes 'The proposed mechanism is solid.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The presented data do not exclude direct mechanical activation of TREK-1, rather suggest a modulation of TREK-1 activity, increasing sensitivity to mechanical inputs, through an inherent mechanosensitivity of PLD2 activity.' All reviewers accept this as a valid mechanism, though they note it is not the only possible activation pathway.

result: Alternative activation mechanisms exist: purified TREK-1 in soy PC does not require the C-terminus for mechanosensitivity, and TREK-1 is directly activated by PA in purified lipids absent stretch. Crude soy extracts contain anionic lipids that may provide PA needed for TREK activation.
evaluation: The editor explicitly notes 'this is only one possible method of channel activation, and mechanisms independent of PLD2 are also probable.' Reviewer 1 states 'It is important to note that this is not the only method of channel activation and that one not involving PLD2 also exists.' Reviewer 2 similarly notes 'The presented data do not exclude direct mechanical activation of TREK-1.' These alternative mechanisms are acknowledged and accepted by all reviewers.

result: TREK-1 activation kinetics: initial currents were observed almost immediately and became significant within 2.1 ms at 60 mmHg pressure. The estimated latency for PLD2-dependent activation is ~650 µs based on diffusion from GM1 to PIP2, which is faster than the instrument setup error (estimated upper limit ~10 ms).
evaluation: These temporal measurements were not challenged by any reviewer. The rapid activation kinetics support the proposed mechanism and are consistent with the spatial reorganization observed. No concerns were raised about the time resolution or the estimates provided.

result: Methodological controls for dSTORM imaging: combined paraformaldehyde and glutaraldehyde fixation effectively inhibited GM1 lipid diffusion (confirmed by FRAP). A two-step fixation procedure was used to minimize artifacts from antibody patching. Slight reduction in GM1 and PIP2 labeling after shear was not statistically significant, and protein movement between domains remains independent of artificial clustering artifacts.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly praises the methodology: 'The use of super-resolution imaging enabled the authors to visualise changes in cluster association that would not have been achievable with diffraction limited microscopy.' The fixation controls and FRAP validation were not challenged. The authors' acknowledgment and control of potential antibody patching artifacts was accepted as adequate.

result: TREK-1 basal current measurements: TREK-1 is a potassium leak channel with inherent basal currents in cultured cells. Basal current was observed both in the presence (16.9 ± 4.3 pA/pF) and absence (24.0 ± 4.2 pA/pF) of xPLD2.
evaluation: These baseline measurements were not questioned by reviewers and serve as important controls for the mechanically evoked current experiments. The data are consistent with established knowledge about TREK-1 as a leak channel.

result: Methodological justifications: HEK293T cells were selected due to minimal endogenous potassium currents. TREK-1 expression was tracked using EGFP tag on the C-terminus, with confirmed surface expression. xPLD2 expression is >10× endogenous PLD2 and outcompetes endogenous PLD2 binding to TREK-1.
evaluation: These methodological choices were not challenged by reviewers. The use of HEK293T cells and the overexpression strategy are standard approaches that were accepted without concern.

result: The mechanism is consistent across multiple cell types (HEK, N2a, C2C12, mouse neurons) despite significant differences in cellular characteristics.
evaluation: This consistency across cell types strengthens the findings and was not challenged. Reviewer 2 notes the work provides insight 'in some cellular systems,' acknowledging the breadth of the experimental approach.

result: Background and established knowledge: TREK-1 is a mechanosensitive K2P channel with analgesic properties. PLD2 interacts with TREK-1 C-terminus and exhibits mechanosensitivity despite lacking a transmembrane domain. Palmitoylation enables PLD2 binding to GM1/cholesterol domains, and mechanical force disrupts this to allow PIP2 interaction. Many signaling molecules and ion channels are palmitoylated and can be targeted to GM1 domains. PIP2 and cholesterol directly modulate many ion channels.
evaluation: These are established facts from prior literature that provide context for the current findings. They were not challenged by reviewers and are well-supported by the citations provided.
